title: Free Elective Study Abroad Credit
description: A series of free academic courses for general elective credit. Students complete a course, when there is not an equivalent SMU course, through an approved SMU Study Abroad program; the grade is included in the SMU GPA. Students can petition to have a FESA course applied toward a specific program or degree requirement. Oversight of FESA courses is provided by SMU's Education Abroad Council.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Bench Aerobics
description: Offers an intense aerobic workout using benches. Also, body contouring using dumb bells, body bars, and mats. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Jogging
description: This class provides an excellent means for improving cardiovascular endurance by running. Introduces selected activities designed to target health-related fitness. Students are expected to increase their jogging ability and set personal running goals.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Weight Training
description: Accommodates all levels of weight training experience. Proper mechanics, safety, and principles of strength building with machines and free weights are presented and practiced. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Weight Training for Women
description: Accommodates all levels of weight training experience. Proper mechanics, safety, principles of strength building, and endurance training with machines and free weights are presented and practiced in a friendly setting. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Individual Fitness
description: Students develop a personal exercise program, and they test and evaluate their own strengths and weaknesses in terms of health and fitness. Accommodates all levels of fitness. Activities aim to improve cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength and endurance, and flexibility.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Walking
description: Walks of 2–2.5 miles during class, and diet and nutrition information. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Beginning Triathlon
description: Students train for a sprint distance triathlon (swim, bike, run) during the term. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness. The $60 activity fee covers triathlon entry.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Intermediate Triathlon
description: Prepares the student to complete an Olympic triathlon (1.5 km swim, 40 km bike ride, and 10 km run). Covers bicycle care, training progressions, and race strategies. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness. The $60 activity fee covers triathlon entry.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of a sprint distance triathlon.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Beginning Marathon Training
description: Students gain the skills and endurance needed to complete the local White Rock Marathon at the end of the term. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness. The $125 activity fee covers marathon entry.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Spinning
description: Spinning utilizes specialized, stationary cycles in a controlled, group setting. This indoor class is uniquely tailored to suit a wide range of abilities. Training principles are inspired by road cycling, and the pace is self-directed. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness. Special activity fee: $10.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Rock Climbing
description: Introduces the sport and fitness of rock climbing. Students learn safety skills and techniques necessary for successful rock climbing and have opportunities to climb outdoors and indoors. Introduces selected activities designed to target health-related fitness. Special activity fee: $50.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Group Fitness
description: This boot camp style class introduces a variety of group fitness activities such as kickboxing, jogging, Pilates, calisthenics, indoor rowing, and strength training.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Pilates
description: Pilates is a total body conditioning exercise method designed to develop the mind and body uniformly. Combines flexibility and strength activities to improve balance, flexibility, and posture and to strengthen core muscles. Aerobic components are included for a full, health-related fitness workout.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Power Yoga
description: Focuses on three main areas of yoga practice: deep breathing, exercise (postures), and meditation. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Judo
description: Judo (“gentle way”) is a safe combat sport that applies maximum efficiency with minimum effort. Students learn the basic skills of judo and techniques for self-defense, particularly against stronger opponents. Also, presents judo’s spiritual aspect of relating to others in more harmonious and effective ways.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Mountain Sports
description: During summer terms, students have the opportunity to participate in a wide range of activities such as hiking, rafting, rock climbing, and fly-fishing. During winter terms, students receive ski and snowboard instruction at the Taos Ski Valley. Students are able to apply the five components of health-related fitness to all of the activities that they pursue. Special activity fee: $800 in summer, $975 in winter to cover all equipment and sports activities. (SMU-in-Taos)

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Intermediate Swimming
description: For the intermediate to advanced swimmer. Provides an opportunity to refine swimming stroke techniques and to gain more advanced swimming skills and aerobic fitness. Includes selected activities designed to target health-related fitness.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Scuba
description: Students need only basic swimming skills to participate. Presents basic physics and physiology (in class) and practical scuba methods and techniques. Includes an introduction to animal behavior so divers can better understand their own behavior underwater. On balance, class time is divided equally among academics, pool work, fitness activities, and open water diving at area lakes. Students earn certification as open water scuba divers upon completion of the course. Special activity fee: $225.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Advanced Scuba
description: Introduces several diving specialties: night diving, wreck diving, search and recovery, and overhead environments. The course is 1/3 academics, 1/3 pool work, and 1/3 open water diving at one of the in-state, area lakes. Also introduces the use of advanced equipment such as lift bags, diver propulsion vehicles, and full-face masks. Students meet experienced and accomplished divers and earn advanced scuba certification upon completion of the class. Fitness activities designed to target health-related fitness are included. Special activity fee: $225.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Self-Defense
description: Teaches students how to prepare physically and mentally for an attack using the ancient Japanese martial art jujitsu and a mix of other martial arts techniques (aikido, judo, kickboxing, and various schools of karate). Includes lessons in blocking, striking, joint locks, release and escape, the proper method of falling, and defense while lying on the ground. Includes fitness activities designed to target health-related fitness.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Basketball
description: Teaches the fundamentals of playing basketball using team drills and offensive and defensive formations and strategy. Augments skill development with game-like conditions. Includes fitness activities designed to target health-related fitness.

title: PRW2: Physical Fitness: Optional
description: Acknowledges the fitness commitments of special groups such as athletes, cheerleaders, pompom squad members, and military service personnel. Students must demonstrate knowledge of health-related fitness concepts and produce an offseason personal fitness plan. Instructor approval required.

title: Honors Sophomore Seminar
description: Honors students work on individual research projects and review the significant resources available to SMU students. Focuses on the liberal arts and science and helps students realize their full academic potential.

title: Creating Your College Experience
description: Designed to guide first year Honors students in a specific scholars Program toward a successful college career, with targeted content per section based on the student’s program. Introductions to key people, services, and opportunities begin the semester, followed by a succession of readings and discussions aimed at helping students thrive at SMU academically, socially, and intellectually. Finally, the course positions students in their new environment with selected readings on Dallas and SMU history and culture.

title: University Honors Humanities Seminar I
description: Offers a study of literature, linguistics, philosophy, psychology, and science that became major modes of interpreting the world in the 20th century and defined what constitutes knowledge in the 21st century. Students must earn a C- or better to pass this course.
prerequisites: Restricted to students in the University Honors Program.

title: University Honors Humanities Seminar II
description: Offers a study of ethical questions derived from history, literature, psychology, and philosophy that focuses on what constitutes a meaningful life. Explores historical challenges to the bases of ethics. This course satisfies the CC Critical Reasoning (CR) Foundation requirement. Students who have already taken another course that fulfills the Critical Reasoning requirement cannot take this course. Students must earn a D- or better to pass this course.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in UHP 2305/WRTR 2305. Restricted to students in the University Honors Program.

title: The Greater Dallas Experience
description: Introduces students to the city of Dallas and the various disciplines studied at SMU. Dallas’s myriad “landscapes” are interrogated and examined in the classroom and in the field.

title: Honors Junior Seminar
description: Designed to guide academically promising students through the process of applying for competitive national and international scholarships and fellowships outside of SMU. Works with students on targeting a scholarship, developing a personal statement, and/or research proposal, as well as preparing for interviews.

title: Second Year Honors Humanities Seminar: The American Citizen - Inclusion & Exclusion
description: Examines the chronology of American history through an interdisciplinary lens with the question of "who is an American" as a thematic focus. Students learn about important moments in American history, and begin to understand the basic chronology of the country, as well as how these key events were understood and experienced by some of the country's most creative and probing minds. The organizing theme of who is an American itself is an important examination of when and where the human rights of the country's inhabitants have been respected--or not respected--over the decades.
prerequisites: Restricted to students in the University Honors Program.

title: STEM Communications
description: Develops students' abilities to convey complex STEM concepts clearly, persuasively, and ethically, whether through written, oral, or visual means. Emphasizes the significance of effective communication in STEM fields, including its role in research dissemination, teamwork, and public engagement.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: One WRTR course from the following: WRTR 1311, WRTR 1312, WRTR 2303, WRTR 2305. Restricted to UHP students only.

title: Cities in Mind
description: When constructing cities, humans have long imagined what an ideal life entails. Over time, the Western city’s primary meaning has shifted, evolving from a political view (the city housing citizens), to a religious emphasis (the city housing a cathedral), to a commercial focus (the city housing a financial center). That evolution leads us to ask, what is a city actually for and how does it define its citizens? This course provides students with a holistic understanding of city life through works of architecture, art, drama, film, history, literature, politics, urban planning, and more. More particularly, the class centers on Dublin, renowned for its literary and urban history. Students who decide to participate receive free travel and accommodation to Dublin during spring break.
prerequisites: Restricted to students in the University Honors Program.

title: Great Books
description: Discusses a range of views on what Great Books are and why they should (or should not) be studied. Students read a varied selection of texts that are traditionally regarded as “Great.” These texts may be literary, philosophical, historical, political, scientific, or mathematical. Each iteration of the course may have a different theme, and therefore a different set of readings semester to semester. By the end of the course, students are better read in Western (or global) cultural tradition, and have a better understanding of why some books do and do not receive the coveted label of “Great.” Restricted to students in the University Honors Program.

title: Queer Studies on the Bible
description: An exploration of the Bible in the context of Queer Studies with special consideration of theology, sociology, and culture.

title: Culture, Religion, and Human Experience
description: Focuses on the theological exploration of spiritual autobiographies, drawing on a variety of sources. This course is for students in the University Honors Program.

title: Honors Oxford Tutorial
description: Adapted from the Oxford University style of education, an in-depth conversation, fueled by intellectual curiosity with a faculty member and a small number of Honors students--its content organized around a professor's area of interest.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Restricted to students in the University Honors Program or with permission of instructor.

title: Honors Independent Study
description: Independent Study on a focused interdisciplinary topic.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Restricted to University Honors students, with junior or senior standing (by hours).

title: First Year Experience Seminar
description: The First Year Experience Seminar supports students’ transition into SMU and prepares students for success at SMU and beyond through self-discovery exercises, exploration of personal values, and introduction to the six Student Affairs learning domains.

title: First Year Research Experience
description: Introduces students to research in a university setting. Discussions include research as a practice, ethics, literature, communication, and networking. This course is limited to students participating in the First Year Research Experience Program.

title: Building Bridges: The Ethics of Service
description: What does it mean to serve others—and how can we do it ethically, across lines of cultural, socioeconomic, and ideological difference? This course encourages students to think critically about the moral complexities of public service. Students explore what it means to act responsibly and respectfully when working with people whose experiences and perspectives may differ significantly from their own. Drawing on classroom learning, case studies, and 10 hours of direct community service, students examine how core values like justice, empathy, and faith and values can guide meaningful service. Students also consider the role that identity, power, and lived experience play in shaping both our intentions and our impact. This is a multicomponent course. Students must register for a one-hour lecture and field studies section. Students participate in their field studies approximately 3-4 times a semester to fulfill their 10 hours of service. Field studies are off site and the time scheduled includes time for travel.

title: Ethics of Information in a Digital Society
description: Explores the ethics of using and sharing information. Considering topics such as AI, news, and privacy, students develop an ethical framework related to authority and evaluation that they can apply in personal, academic, and professional contexts.

title: Academic Success and Personal Development
description: A graded course designed to help students improve reading efficiency, executive functioning, and lifelong learning skills.

title: Success Strategies
description: Students learn study skills and other strategies for creating success in their academic, professional, and personal lives. Includes self-assessment and journal writing to identify academic strengths and challenges. Provides an opportunity to explore the campus resources to succeed at SMU.

title: Personal Finance and Branding
description: Students develop a comprehensive understanding of financial management principles and personal branding strategies in order to develop a strong personal brand to enhance their career prospects.

title: Career Discovery
description: Provides course credit for students completing the Career Discovery program through Podium Education. Through this program, students learn about NACE career competency-aligned workplace and experience themes. Over a single term, students engage in hands-on projects with a variety of diverse organizations across industries, including established organizations, innovative ventures, and nonprofits. Students experience first-hand what it is like to work in high-demand fields and across a wide range of organizations and career functions, demonstrating how multiple academic paths can lead to meaningful careers. With a mix of asynchronous content, weekly live sessions, and exposure to real companies and professionals, students gain resume-worthy experience, benefit from career coaching, and reflect on their strengths and interests.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Participation in the Career Discovery Program through Podium Education.

title: Introduction to Mock Trial
description: Enhances students’ knowledge of the American adversarial judicial system through in-depth study of trial procedure and evidentiary rules. The primary teaching vehicle is a simulated trial based on the official hypothetical case published by the American Mock Trial Association for the current school year. Cases alternate between criminal and civil cases. Students must complete the course to be eligible to participate on the Mock Trial team.

title: Academic Explorations and Career Readiness
description: Equips students with essential career development and academic planning skills to navigate their academic and professional journeys with confidence. Students explore major and career pathways, develop career readiness competencies, and gain hands-on experience with job and internship search strategies, including resume writing and networking. Additionally, students receive guidance on course selection, Common Curriculum navigation, and how to maximize career counseling and academic advising resources. Through interactive discussions and practical exercises, students build a strong foundation for academic success and career advancement.

title: Where Research Begins
description: Students brainstorm ideas and write a robust proposal for a research project that can be used in applications for internal fellowships and departmental distinction. The course is based around the book Where Research Begins by Mullaney and Rea.

title: Advanced Personal Finance and Branding
description: Students develop reasoning skills to make decisions regarding their personal finances. In addition, students learn the importance of networking and establishing a personal brand for career advancement.

title: Special Topics
description: Covers topics that have temporary or limited interest and that support students' personal, academic, or leadership development. Topics vary by instructor and are approved by the department.

title: Diversity: Fitting Into a World of Difference
description: This course is a study of human diversity and identity development. Students learn about their own identities and about fitting into the communities of which they are a part. Topics include elements of oppression, cycle of socialization, identity development models, privilege, race, sex, gender, sexuality, ability, ethnicity, class, and faith.

title: Special Topics
description: Covers topics that have temporary or limited interest and that support students' personal, academic, or leadership development. Topics vary by instructor and are approved by the department.

title: Information Systems and Society
description: Presents technological advances in information systems of the late 20th to 21st centuries and their impact on society’s creation, evaluation, and sharing of knowledge. Critical information studies considers how inventions like the Internet, social media, algorithms, and artificial intelligence change epistemology, searching behavior, reading and attention, the news, and mis/disinformation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: A course that satisfies the CC Critical Reasoning (CR) Foundations requirement.

title: The Art and Science of Game Design
description: Explores how Generative AI has emerged as a design tool through the production of creative artifacts in digital game development. Students apply conventions of the art form of interactivity within the context of videogame design and production. Student teams use a 2D platformer game starter-kit with 2D art, C# scripts, and a licensed sound library, alongside a local instance of generative AI in order to expand the experiences of creativity in the theories of interactive media and in a classic videogame genre. Students participate in lectures and hands-on seminar discussion collaborations, team-based lab workshops, and complete a digital game group project. This course explores how mixed media technologies are changing the way we learn, work, play, teach, and communicate. It is a hands-on course in which the students learn how to use mixed media technology applications for the production of creative artifacts. Basic computer skills are recommended, but no computer programming or graphics skills are required.

title: From IM to AI: How People Learn with Technology
description: This course explores how adult students learn in universities and offers a special focus on how technology changes the way we learn. Students examine learning technologies from the rise of the internet to today’s powerful AI tools and dive into real-world examples of technology in college classrooms and think critically about its benefits and challenges. Students engage in big-picture questions about ethics, academic integrity, and the future of learning. Through hands-on activities, discussions, and guest speaker experts, students learn how to apply key ideas about learning to their experiences and assess AI’s role in their learning process. Students develop the skills to work with classmates and professors in technology-enhanced learning environments. By the end of the course, students are able to explain major educational ideas, analyze AI’s impact on learning, and use AI tools to support their academic and career goals. This course is designed for students interested in the past and future of education and technology--and how AI can help (or complicate) learning in universities.

title: Asset-Based Human Development
description: This course introduces the field of psychology, with emphasis on how people deal with the problems and challenges of everyday life. Students learn about classical and contemporary theories, recent research, and applications of the science of psychology to everyday situations.

title: Special Topics
description: Covers topics that have temporary or limited interest and that support students' personal, academic, or leadership development. Topics vary by instructor and are approved by the department.

title: Rediscovering Leadership
description: Introduces first-year students to leadership opportunities at SMU and the skills they need to succeed in leadership roles.
prerequisites: Restricted to Hunt Leadership Scholars only.

title: Comparative Leadership
description: Introduces students to leadership and organizational change theories, and applies these theories to education systems and policy in the United States and abroad. Leadership and educational systems are analyzed and compared, enhanced by educational visits abroad to provide context and framework for comparison and synthesis. Students in the Hunt Leadership Scholars Program only.

title: Self, Identity, and Community Engagement
description: Students examine their values, beliefs, and identities; the ways in which these factors influence engagement and interaction with others; and how these qualities and characteristics can help students more effectively serve their communities.

title: Personal Responsibility and Community
description: Students examine how personal mindsets, choices, behaviors, and outcomes impact their lives, other people’s lives, and their communities. Through coursework grounded in the Assets-Based Community Development Model, students are challenged to think critically about the effect of values, beliefs, and identities on how they engage with others and their communities at large. In a semester-long community engagement project, students learn about themselves and others, apply class content to a community need, and reflect on the experience through a process that can benefit them throughout their lives.

title: Change Makers: Exploring Social Justice in Civic Leadership
description: This three-hour course explores how identity, power, and community shape civic life both in the United States and around the world. Students examine leadership, migration, social movements, and resilience across regions including Latin America, Africa, the Middle East, and Europe, while connecting theory to practice through community engagement, guest speakers, and site visits. Along the way, students develop transferable skills in ethical reasoning, collaboration, and civic leadership - tools that are valuable for future careers and for making a meaningful impact beyond the classroom.

title: Advanced Trial Advocacy
description: Explores the American adversarial judiciary system at the trial court level. Students gain an in-depth understanding of the trial process, trial procedure, introduction and suppression of evidence, and the necessary advocacy skills to present both civil and criminal case problems. The fact pattern for purposes of simulating trial is governed by the hypothetical case problem published by the American Mock Trial Association ("AMTA") for the current school year. The AMTA problem alternates between criminal and civil cases. The AMTA problem is not only utilized in the classroom but is also the problem used throughout the school year for purposes of competitions for the SMU Mock Trial team. Students use the skills learned in class and apply them during actual mock trial competition.

title: Fundamentals of Academic Research
description: Provides an overview of academic research methodology including the basic concepts of quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and applied projects as well as an understanding of ethical considerations. Students critically read academic journal articles to identify research methodology, frame research studies based on a series of prompts, and integrate a tightly-focused, self-selected series of articles into an abbreviated literature review.

title: Career Development Internship Experience
description: Provides an in-depth, hands-on experience in a multidisciplinary project through the Global Career Accelerator. Students work together on real-world projects sourced from global companies, allowing them to work collaboratively with peers from different countries and cultures. Through this internship experience, students develop and apply skills to solve real-world, career-oriented problems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Registration in the Global Career Accelerator through Podium Education.

title: Internship
description: Students from any major can earn academic credit for supervised internship experiences in business, government, or non-profit settings. title: Leadership for an Uncertain World
description: Introduces a conscious, introspective, and holistic approach to leading self and others in a chaotic, rapidly changing and uncertain world. Specific emphasis is placed on the importance of self-knowledge, mindfulness, and the creation of positive team environments through intentional human connection. The course also includes health, fitness, and wilderness experiential components with a focus on wilderness ethics/Leave No Trace (LNT) principles. Through LNT students explore ways to minimize impact on natural environments and LNT application to individual urban surroundings, community and personal choices. Course fee: $1,000 covers and insures room and board at SMU’s campus in Taos, outdoor rental equipment, and payment for wilderness guide(s).

title: Interdisciplinary Critical Thought
description: Students engage in critical thought in the context of career readiness. They reflect on and apply key concepts from their areas of concentration to seminar discussions, activities, and assessments. Course materials and assignments help them analyze, conceptualize, interpret, synthesize, or evaluate information, and ground their work in appropriate internal evidence or external sources. This is a project-based capstone course that focuses on real world problems and professional goals.

title: Integrative Leadership in Practice
description: This capstone course provides interdisciplinary studies majors with an immersive, high-impact experience focused on developing ethical, inclusive, and adaptive leadership for complex professional environments. Students integrate knowledge from their individualized academic pathways to refine a personal leadership philosophy, build collaborative communication skills, and apply interdisciplinary thinking to multifaceted organizational challenges. Through applied leadership labs, reflective practice, team-based simulations, and a culminating interdisciplinary project, students strengthen their capacity to lead with integrity, engage effectively across diverse teams, and translate theory into practice. The course emphasizes ethical reasoning, communication excellence, emotional intelligence, and systems thinking, preparing students to navigate VUCA (volatile, uncertain, complex, ambiguous) environments and contribute meaningfully in early-career roles.
